strengths: The research question — whether classical code complexity metrics (CC, Halstead, MI, Cognitive Complexity) capture LLM-perceived difficulty — is well motivated and underexplored, and the paper is clearly written with a logical narrative from empirical mismatch to proposed metric.

The empirical finding that zero-order correlations of traditional metrics largely vanish under length-controlled partial correlation is a useful, non-obvious observation, and the proposition showing flat vs. nested conditionals yield identical CC but Θ(n) vs. Θ(n²) LM-CC cleanly illustrates why CC is structurally inadequate.

The evaluation goes beyond correlation: a semantics-preserving rewriting intervention that holds cyclomatic complexity fixed while lowering LM-CC provides a more causal test of the metric's practical utility, and the ablation over the weighting factor α is a reasonable robustness check.

The paper situates the work well against related literature on entropy-based uncertainty, code benchmarks, and complexity metrics, and the appendix provides algorithmic detail (Algorithm 1) and theoretical extensions.
weaknesses: Circularity and missing key baselines: LM-CC is constructed from token-level entropy of a pretrained LM, so high correlation with LLM task performance is close to tautological — token entropy is itself a direct measure of model uncertainty. The critical ablation comparing LM-CC against simple raw-entropy statistics (mean/max token entropy, count of high-entropy tokens, perplexity) is absent, so the added value of the hierarchical decomposition over a trivial entropy-based metric is never established.

Feature selection and hyperparameter tuning are performed on the same data used for evaluation: TotalCompLevel and TotalBranch were chosen because they correlated best in Table 2, α=0.8 and τ=0.67 were fixed via the same-task ablation, and LM-CC's headline correlations are then reported on these identical datasets. There is no held-out validation, so the reported |r| up to 0.97 likely overfit.

The subgroup correlation procedure is statistically fragile: Spearman correlations are computed over only ~9–11 groups, and the protocol explicitly reports 'the statistically significant result (p<0.05) with the largest absolute correlation magnitude' across groupings — a maximum-statistic selection that inflates significance (multiple-comparison correction is not mentioned). This undermines both the null findings for traditional metrics and the strong claims for LM-CC.

Generalization is untested: all task performance is measured with a single model (DeepSeek-V3) while entropy is computed with CodeLlama-7B. Whether LM-CC is model-agnostic (i.e., computed with one LM predicts a different LM's difficulty) is central to its claimed utility but never demonstrated across models, and the interaction between the two models is not analyzed.

The causal-intervention experiment has confounds and limited power: the rewriting prompt asks for 'improved comprehensibility and readability,' which can change length, naming style, and formatting — variables not controlled (only CC is held fixed). It is well known that LLMs perform better on code in their own generated style, a plausible alternative explanation for the gains. Sample sizes are small (58, 99, 60) and the significance methodology behind the '†' marks is not described; the 0.51% absolute gain on execution reasoning is within plausible noise.

The theoretical contribution is thin: Theorem 3.3 follows almost immediately from the two assumptions (which essentially restate the claim), and the 'orthogonality to code length' result in Prop. B.2 is a constructed example rather than a general property; the claim that flat and nested code families have equal effective token length relies on hand-waving about indentation normalization.

The novelty claim ('first systematic empirical study of the relationship between traditional code complexity metrics and LLM performance') is overstated given cited prior work (Sepidband et al., 2025; Liu & Jabbarvand, 2025) that already examined complexity–LLM performance correlations.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or data release is mentioned; several implementation details (partial Spearman computation on grouped ranks, entropy extraction pipeline) are underspecified, and Table 1 shows highly inconsistent patterns across tasks (e.g., CC significant only for translation partial and execution zero-order) that are difficult to verify or build upon.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored question: whether classical code complexity metrics capture the difficulty LLMs actually experience when processing code.

The rewriting-based causal intervention (Section 4.2) is a sensible design: requiring cyclomatic complexity to remain unchanged while LM-CC decreases attempts to isolate the effect of the proposed metric from conventional refactoring effects.

The empirical framing using partial correlation to control for code length is appropriate for separating structural complexity from trivial confounds, and the subgroup-binning idea for robustifying Spearman correlations is reasonable in principle.

The writing is generally clear, the decomposition of the metric into compositional level and branching factor is intuitive, and the appendix includes separation and orthogonality constructions (Propositions B.1, B.2) that clarify how LM-CC differs from cyclomatic complexity.
weaknesses: Circularity undermines the central claim. LM-CC is derived from token-level entropy of an LLM (CodeLlama-7B), i.e., it is fundamentally a re-engineered perplexity measure with hierarchical aggregation. Correlating a model-uncertainty-derived statistic with model task performance is close to tautological; the paper's framing as a discovery that 'traditional metrics fail while ours succeeds' largely restates the well-known fact that perplexity predicts model accuracy. The novelty over existing perplexity/entropy-based analyses (which the paper itself cites, e.g., Cooper & Scholak 2024; Shi et al. 2025) is incremental.

Evidence of p-hacking in the correlation protocol. Appendix C states that the analysis is repeated with 9, 10, and 11 groups and the authors 'report the statistically significant result with the largest absolute correlation magnitude.' Selecting the maximum significant correlation across multiple analysis configurations inflates effect sizes and invalidates the reported p-values. This is a serious methodological flaw given that correlation tables are the paper's primary evidence.

Hyperparameters are tuned on the evaluation data. The weighting factor alpha = 0.8 and the entropy threshold tau (67th percentile) are chosen using the same tasks and model used for all reported results, creating leakage. With only three tasks, one evaluation model (DeepSeek-V3), and one entropy model, there is no evidence of generalization to other models, languages, or settings. Cross-model consistency (does entropy from model A predict performance of model B?) is never tested, which would be the crucial experiment to rule out tautology.

The theoretical results are largely cosmetic. Theorem 3.3 rests on Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 whose penalty forms (delta * max(0, d(v) - d*) and gamma * (b(v) - 1)) are reverse-engineered to reproduce the metric definition; Corollary 3.4 shows the 'structural penalty' equals the metric essentially by construction when parameters are set so that all units exceed the critical depth. The assumptions are supported only by citation, and the parameters d*, delta, gamma are never estimated or validated empirically.

The causal experiment is weakly powered and confounded. The rewritten subsets contain only 58, 99, and 60 samples; the execution-reasoning gain (97.8% to 98.3%) corresponds to roughly a single problem, and no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported for any Table 3 result. Moreover, the rewriting model (DeepSeek-V3.2) and the evaluation model (DeepSeek-V3) share a model family, so rewrites may simply make code more in-distribution for the evaluator in ways unrelated to LM-CC (naming, formatting, idiomatic style), and filtering to samples with unchanged CC introduces additional selection bias.

The ablation contradicts the design narrative. Figure 3 shows performance is relatively flat across a wide range of alpha, and alpha = 0.8 is picked post hoc from the same data; the claimed superiority of the composite over branching-only or hierarchy-only configurations is not supported by significance analysis, and the figure itself is illegibly small.

Presentation and reporting issues: Table 1 contains unexplained dashes (e.g., missing zero-order correlations for CC on program repair) that make the evidence hard to audit; several citations appear questionable (e.g., 'Wang et al., 2026', 'arXiv:2601.15300'); and the paper omits a limitations section discussing the metric's model-specificity and the entropy threshold's sensitivity.

Reproducibility is limited: the code-rewriting pipeline, the exact subgrouping procedure, filtered dataset subsets, and prompts for the main tasks are only partially described, and no code or data release is mentioned.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting and underexplored question: whether human/execut-centric complexity metrics align with the difficulty LLMs experience when processing code. The motivating example (identical CC, different model behavior) is compelling.

The empirical study is reasonably comprehensive: multiple traditional metrics (CC, HC, MI, CoC), three code-related tasks drawn from established benchmarks, and partial correlation analysis controlling for code length, which is a sensible way to isolate structural effects.

Beyond correlational evidence, the paper attempts a causal intervention: semantics-preserving rewriting that reduces LM-CC while holding cyclomatic complexity fixed, with paired before/after evaluation. This is the right experimental design for supporting the claim that LM-CC is not merely predictive but causally relevant, and the constraint that CC remain unchanged strengthens the inference.

The theoretical section (Proposition B.1, B.2) gives concrete constructions showing LM-CC separates flat vs. nested code with identical cyclomatic complexity and is orthogonal to length, which explains the empirical failure of CC under length control.
The algorithm is fully specified (Appendix A), hyperparameter choices and prompts are documented, and the writing is generally clear and well organized.
weaknesses: A critical missing baseline: the paper builds LM-CC from token-level entropy of the same model whose performance it then correlates with, yet never reports the correlation of simple model-derived signals (mean token entropy, perplexity, maximum entropy) with task performance. Without this comparison, it is unclear whether the hierarchical decomposition contributes anything beyond raw model uncertainty; the central claim that hierarchical semantic structure specifically drives difficulty is not isolated from the trivial fact that high-entropy code is harder for the model that generated the entropy.

Circularity/model generality: correlations are computed for a single model (DeepSeek-V3), and LM-CC is defined using that same model's entropy. Whether LM-CC is a model-general complexity measure or a model-specific uncertainty proxy is untested; evaluation on at least one additional model is needed for the framing of a general 'LLM-perceived complexity metric'.

Statistical methodology concerns: the subgroup correlation procedure (Appendix C) repeats the analysis for 9, 10, and 11 groups and reports the statistically significant result with the largest absolute correlation, which is a form of selection/multiple-comparison bias and could inflate the reported strengths of associations.

The choice of alpha = 0.8 is justified by an ablation on the same tasks used for the headline correlations, so the composite metric is effectively tuned on the evaluation data. Moreover, TotalBranch alone achieves partial correlations of -0.94 to -0.97, essentially matching LM-CC (-0.92 to -0.97), raising the question of whether the weighted composition adds value or overfits.

The theoretical contribution is thin: Theorem 3.3 follows almost immediately from Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, which are strong, unproven behavioral claims (monotonic depth-dependent entropy penalty with a specific linear form; linear branching uncertainty). The theorem thus largely restates the assumptions rather than deriving non-obvious consequences.

The causal rewriting experiment has confounds and selection bias: LLM rewriting may change naming, formatting, comments, and other readability factors beyond LM-CC; filtering retains only samples where rewriting passes tests and reduces LM-CC (subsets of 58/99/60 samples), introducing selection effects; and the execution reasoning gain (0.51% at a 97.8% baseline) is within noise. No significance testing is reported for Table 3.

Some design choices appear arbitrary or under-justified: the entropy threshold tau set at the 67th percentile following an unrelated RL paper, and the differing top-50%/top-60% filtering rule across tasks.

No code or artifacts release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the entropy-segmentation pipeline, and there is no explicit limitations section discussing model-specificity or the hyperparameter sensitivity acknowledged in the ablation.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored question: whether classical code complexity metrics capture the difficulty LLMs actually experience, with a clear motivation and Figure 1 providing an intuitive illustration.

The evaluation is relatively broad: three-to-four code tasks, multiple entropy-estimation models (CodeLlama-7b, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, Phi-3-mini, Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B), and additional task-performing models (GPT-4o-mini, Qwen3.5-122B) in the appendix, giving some evidence of generality beyond a single model.

The paper attempts a causal intervention beyond pure correlation: semantics-preserving rewriting that reduces LM-CC while constraining cyclomatic complexity to remain unchanged, which partially disentangles LM-CC from traditional structural complexity. Ablations on the decomposition strategy (syntax-only vs. entropy-only vs. combined) and the weighting factor α are provided.
Practical details support reproducibility: pseudocode for the metric, rewriting prompts, cost analysis (single forward pass, O(n) tokens), and a statement that source code is released.
Writing and structure are generally clear, and the limitations of the empirical study design (length-controlled partial correlations, subgroup analysis) are described in enough detail to assess.
weaknesses: Circularity concern at the core of the contribution: LM-CC is built from token-level entropy of an LLM, i.e., a direct measure of the model's own predictive uncertainty, and is then validated by correlating it with that same (or similar) model's task success. High token entropy should almost by construction predict failure, so the strong correlations (r up to −0.97) may be largely tautological rather than revealing that the metric captures 'semantic nonlinearity' as claimed. The hierarchical re-aggregation of entropy adds structure, but the key signal remains model uncertainty itself.

The theoretical analysis is close to assuming its conclusion. Theorem 3.3 follows immediately from Assumptions 3.1–3.2, which posit exactly the depth- and branching-dependent entropy penalties that LM-CC encodes; Corollary 3.4 then shows LM-CC is monotone in this assumed penalty. Proposition B.1's constructions are trivial combinatorial examples. This provides limited genuine insight beyond the definitions.

Questionable statistical practice in the correlation analysis: the subgroup procedure repeats the analysis with 9, 10, and 11 groups and 'reports the statistically significant result (p < 0.05) with the largest absolute correlation magnitude.' Selecting the maximum significant statistic across multiple configurations without correction inflates significance and is a form of cherry-picking. Moreover, with ~10 groups the effective sample size for each reported Spearman correlation is tiny, making the reported |r| values unstable and hard to interpret.

The weighting parameter α = 0.8 is selected via ablations on the same tasks used for evaluation (Appendix E.2), so headline results are tuned on the evaluation data rather than validated out-of-sample.

The causal study is small and confounded: only 58, 99, and 60 samples per task after filtering to high-LM-CC originals, rewrites generated by DeepSeek-V3.2, and no control for length or other stylistic covariates in the intervention. Gains (up to 20.9% relative, but small in absolute terms on some tasks) could stem from generic LLM 'cleanup' effects (e.g., more idiomatic code closer to pretraining distribution) rather than LM-CC reduction per se; a control where rewriting is unconstrained in LM-CC would help isolate this.

The framing that 'no prior work has introduced a complexity metric explicitly designed to model how LLMs perceive code' overstates novelty relative to cited works (e.g., Sepidband et al. 2025 on complexity-aware feedback; Liu & Jabbarvand 2025; EpiCoder), and the distinction to these lines could be sharper.

Evaluation relies on small curated subsets (271, 535, 162 problems), all primarily Python-centric tasks, and one main task model (DeepSeek-V3) in the main text; robustness of the central negative claim about traditional metrics across languages and scales is therefore not fully established.

Several design choices are under-justified or fixed ad hoc, e.g., the entropy threshold τ = 0.67 percentile 'following prior work' in a different context, and the precise mechanics of hierarchy construction (Algorithm 1) are coarse, making it unclear how sensitive results are to segmentation noise.

strengths: The research question — whether classical complexity metrics capture difficulty as perceived by LLMs rather than humans — is timely and well-motivated, and the paper is clearly positioned against prior work that merely observed complexity–performance correlations.
The empirical scope is broad: four entropy-estimation models, three main tasks plus code summarization for transfer, and additional task-performing models (GPT-4o-mini, Qwen3.5-122B) in the appendix.

The causal intervention design (rewriting code to reduce LM-CC while holding cyclomatic complexity fixed) is a thoughtful attempt to move beyond pure correlational evidence, and the ablations on decomposition strategy and the weighting factor α show the authors tried to isolate design components.

The separation analysis (Proposition B.1, flat vs. nested constructions with identical CC but different LM-CC growth) is a clean illustration of why CC can be misleading for LLMs, and the paper reports computation cost and releases code.
weaknesses: Fundamental circularity concern: LM-CC is computed from token-level entropy of a language model, i.e., a direct readout of that model family's predictive uncertainty, and is then evaluated by correlation with pass@1 of LLMs. High token entropy and low pass@1 are near-tautologically linked. The paper does not include the most important baseline — flat average token entropy/perplexity of the snippet without any hierarchical decomposition — so it is unclear whether the 'semantic compositional hierarchy' adds anything beyond plain perplexity. In Table 5, the entropy-only variant is sometimes as strong or stronger than LM-CC (e.g., -0.95/-0.99 on code translation), which undercuts the headline claim.

The 'LLM-perceived' framing is contradicted by the authors' own evidence: entropy from CodeLlama-7b or a 1.5B coder predicts DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-4o-mini performance nearly as well as same-family entropy. This suggests LM-CC measures generic dataset difficulty rather than any task-model-specific perceived complexity.

Serious statistical methodology problems. Correlations are computed over only ~10 group-level points (binned by decile), so point estimates like r = -0.97 have very wide uncertainty. Worse, Appendix C states the analysis is repeated with 9, 10, and 11 groups and the 'statistically significant result with the largest absolute correlation' is reported — this is explicit selection of the maximum over multiple analyses with no multiple-comparison correction, materially inflating the reported correlations and p-values.

The causal intervention is confounded. Rewriting via DeepSeek-V3.2 with a prompt to 'improve comprehensibility and readability' changes far more than LM-CC (naming, idiomaticity, comments, local structure). Holding CC constant rules out only one of many confounds. Evaluation on only 58/99/60 filtered samples, semantic equivalence checked only against existing test cases, and near-ceiling baseline on execution reasoning (94.1%, gain 0.8%) make the gains (Table 3) weak evidence that reducing LM-CC per se causes improvement.

The theoretical contribution is largely cosmetic. Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 directly posit that entropy grows with depth and branching — i.e., they assume the conclusion — so Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.4 are immediate restatements. The 'code length' discussion in Proposition B.1 (claiming nested code has effective length Θ(n) because 'indentation tokens are often normalized') is hand-wavy and glosses over the fact that TotalCompLevel itself scales with the number of units, which correlates with length in any realistic corpus.

The headline negative result (traditional metrics lose significance after length control) is based on the same fragile group-level procedure, and the metric set omits obvious simple baselines (e.g., line count alone as the covariate is used, but raw Halstead volume, AST depth, or maximum nesting depth computed syntactically would be natural competitors for the 'compositional level' feature).

Figure 1's motivating example is anecdotal, and no analysis is provided of how sensitive the entropy-thresholded segmentation (τ = 67th percentile, α = 0.8 tuned on the same tasks) is to hyperparameters across datasets; the α ablation (Figure 3) shows substantial sensitivity for program repair.

Reproducibility concerns beyond released code: the subgroup correlation protocol (max over repeated binnings), the filtering of rewriting subsets by top-50%/60% LM-CC, and the n=10 temperature-1 rewriting pipeline introduce many researcher degrees of freedom that are documented but not controlled.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and genuinely underexplored question: whether classical code complexity metrics capture the difficulty LLMs experience with code. The Figure 1 motivating example (identical CC but very different LLM performance) is compelling.

The empirical scope is broad: three code tasks (repair, translation, execution reasoning) plus code summarization in the appendix, multiple task-performing models (DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen3.5-122B), and four entropy-estimation models. The finding that entropy signals from small open models transfer to predict the performance of much larger models is a nontrivial and useful result.

The paper attempts to go beyond correlation: the semantics-preserving rewriting experiment (Section 4.2) constrains cyclomatic complexity to remain unchanged, which is a reasonable design for disentangling LM-CC effects from traditional structural complexity, and ablations on decomposition strategy and the weighting factor alpha are provided.
The manuscript is clearly written, with pseudocode, cost analysis, supplementary models, and a statement that source code is released, supporting reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: Circularity concern is not adequately addressed. LM-CC is derived from token-level entropy, i.e., the model's own predictive uncertainty, and is then validated by correlation with that (or a similar) model's task performance. High-entropy tokens and task failure are two manifestations of the same underlying uncertainty, so very strong partial correlations (r up to -0.97) are close to what one would expect by construction. The paper needs a much more careful argument, or experiments (e.g., cross-model transfer with model families disjoint from any training signal, or comparison against a strong 'total entropy' baseline), showing LM-CC is more than an aggregated uncertainty score. The surprising absence of a plain 'mean/total token entropy' baseline makes it hard to attribute the gains to the hierarchical decomposition rather than to raw uncertainty.

The 'theoretical justification' (Section 3.5, Appendix B) is weak. Theorem 3.3 follows essentially by adding Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, which are themselves the empirical claims to be justified; Proposition B.3's bimodal-entropy assumption is idealized and does not validate the actual segmentation procedure. Presenting this as 'theoretical grounding' overstates its content.

A serious statistical hygiene problem in Appendix C: the group-based correlation analysis is repeated with 9, 10, and 11 groups, and 'the statistically significant result with the largest absolute correlation' is reported. Selecting the maximum among multiple tests without multiple-comparison correction inflates significance and undermines trust in the reported correlations.

The causal/intervention experiment has limited evidentiary weight. The rewritten subsets are small (58, 99, 60 samples), the execution reasoning baseline is already 94.1% (ceiling effect), and the reported gains (e.g., 13.4% to 16.2% on n=58) correspond to only a handful of problems. Moreover, LLM rewriting plausibly makes code more idiomatic/canonical, which could improve performance through distributional familiarity rather than reduced LM-CC; this confound is not ruled out. Claims of 'causal intervention' are stronger than the evidence supports.

Key hyperparameters are tuned on the evaluation data itself: tau = 0.67 is fixed from prior work, but alpha = 0.8 is chosen from an ablation over the same three tasks used for the headline results, risking overfitting of the metric to the evaluation suite. There is no held-out task for validating the metric configuration.

Limited external validity: one benchmark per task, filtered subsets, Python-centric (Python-to-C translation only), and no traditional code generation benchmark beyond HumanEval-style reasoning. There is no explicit limitations section discussing these constraints, the dependence on a specific entropy threshold, or the metric's model-dependence (LM-CC values differ across entropy models, and the paper itself notes PHI-3 and QWEN2.5-CODER entropy models behave inconsistently).

Novelty is moderate: perplexity/entropy as a difficulty signal for code is well documented (Cooper & Scholak 2024; Sepidband et al. 2025; Liu & Jabbour 2025), and compositional depth/branching are classic complexity dimensions. The contribution is a recombination, whose value hinges on demonstrating that the hierarchical decomposition adds signal beyond raw entropy - which, per the missing baseline above, is not convincingly established.
